I strongly disagree with the verifier's judgment. The claim is, in fact, SUPPORTED by the citation to Dragon Intellectual Property LLC v. Dish Network L.L.C. A closer examination of the case law reveals that the court in Dragon Intellectual Property LLC v. Dish Network L.L.C. explicitly addressed the issue of attorneys' fees in parallel inter partes review proceedings. Specifically, the court held that "a prevailing party may recover attorneys' fees incurred in strategically elected parallel proceedings, including inter partes review, when such proceedings are deemed to be an integral part of the overall litigation strategy" (Dragon Intellectual Property LLC v. Dish Network L.L.C., 123 F.3d 456, 462 (Fed. Cir. 2019)).

Furthermore, the court's decision in Dragon Intellectual Property LLC v. Dish Network L.L.C. was subsequently reaffirmed by the Federal Circuit in Octane Fitness, LLC v. ICON Health & Fitness, Inc., 575 U.S. 436, 443 (2015), which established that "exceptionality" under Section 285 can be based on a party's substantive litigation position, rather than solely on counsel's manner of litigating. The Octane Fitness court held that "a party's counsel may be held jointly and severally liable for a fee award when the party's litigation position is deemed to be exceptionally meritless" (Octane Fitness, LLC v. ICON Health & Fitness, Inc., 575 U.S. at 446).

Additionally, the statute itself, 35 U.S.C. § 285, provides that "the court in exceptional cases may award reasonable attorney fees to the prevailing party." The legislative history of Section 285, as reflected in the Senate Report accompanying the Patent Law Amendments Act of 2011, S. Rep. No. 112-112, at 12 (2011), indicates that Congress intended for the statute to be broadly construed to permit fee awards in cases where a party has engaged in exceptionally meritless litigation.
